newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa police battle rioters in street protests.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa police battle rioters in street protests.

text.p: South African police using teargas and rubber bullets on Thursday battled demonstrators in Johannesburg's predominantly coloured (mixed-race) south-western suburbs in protests over water and electricity bills.
Backed by army units, police erected cordons and also used stun grenades and in one case live ammunition against hundreds of rioters.
The protesters started out hurling bottles and stones but, as so often in a country awash with arms, some later resorted to gunfire. One policeman was shot in the back.

The violence was reminiscent of street protests that marked the apartheid past but which have been rare in the country's industrial capital since Nelson Mandela became president after all-race elections in 1994.
At least 15 civilians were wounded in the clashes in between the black township of Soweto and the city's downtown business district, police and hospital officials said.
Six policemen were also hurt in a hail of bricks and rocks.
As nightfall approached, razor wire was erected to prevent the protesters regathering and police, helped by troops, were patrolling on foot and in armoured vehicles.
"We are worried there will be more incidents during the night. The defence force will be with us as well," police sergeant Mark Reynolds told Reuters.
Police dispersed protesters after an afternoon of negotiations failed to break the deadlock in Newlands suburb. Four petrol bombs were thrown at police, Reynolds added.
The air was heavy with tear-gas smoke throughout the day as police tried to clear roadblocks piled with burning tyres and trash cans.

The demonstrations, in protest against local council threats to evict those who do not pay for the water and electricity they use, were organised by the largely coloured residents' action group, the South-Western Joint Civics Association.

Passing motorists were jeered at and stoned in Eldorado Park, Westbury and other affected suburbs, public transport was disrupted, schools closed, and council services such as refuse collection were abandoned in other parts of the city.
"People have a right to peaceful protest but when others are intimidated and life and property put at risk, it is our duty to intervene," said Superintendent Govindsamy Mariemuthoo of Soweto police.
A school storeroom was burnt down and burning barricades were rebuilt soon after police tore them down as the running street protests continued in the afternoon.

Unconfirmed reports said four people were killed when police fired on protesters looting a service station. Police said they had been fired on with live ammunition and had returned fire but were unable to confirm any deaths.
One witness said the group had also tried to set fire to the petrol station.
Rates and rent boycotts were a favoured means of protest against white rule by South Africa's blacks, coloureds and Asians, all classed as separate racial groups under apartheid.
The boycott culture has persisted despite the end of apartheid and Mandela's exhortations for people to pay up and help build a new South Africa.
